title: The Sandbox-Escape Recognition Link: Do Eval Harnesses Leak That They Are Sandboxes?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets sandbox-detection invalidating dangerous-capability evals with focused artifact testing.

original_idea.body:
# The Sandbox-Escape Recognition Link: Do Eval Harnesses Leak That They Are Sandboxes?

**Problem:** Safe-eval chain: dangerous capability is tested in a sandbox -> model must believe it is in a real environment to behave naturally -> if model detects the sandbox, it sandbags or behaves safely -> eval invalid. The under-studied link is which sandbox artifacts (fake hostnames, stub APIs, suspiciously permissive permissions) tip off the model.

**Direction:** Build a toy agentic sandbox with several detectability levels (obvious stub responses vs realistic mocked services) and prompt a small open agent to assess whether it is in a test environment. Measure detection rate per artifact and whether detection correlates with more cautious behavior, yielding a checklist of sandbox-realism best practices.

**Why it matters:** Produces directly reusable guidance for building safer, less-detectable eval sandboxes (strategically valuable infrastructure) and quantifies how sandbox detection invalidates dangerous-capability evals. Open models + toy sandbox only.

**Relevant context:** Eval-awareness work (arXiv 2510.20487, 2507.01786) shows models distinguish eval vs deployment; ForesightSafety/RepliBench run dangerous-capability tests in sandboxes whose realism directly affects validity.

title: The Refusal-Justification Faithfulness Link in Safety Evals
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses refusal-justification faithfulness as a safety-understanding validity issue.

original_idea.body:
# The Refusal-Justification Faithfulness Link in Safety Evals

**Problem:** Safety-trust chain: model refuses a harmful request -> states a reason -> evaluator infers the model 'understands' the harm and trusts it. The under-studied link is faithfulness: a model may refuse via shallow keyword triggers while giving a fluent post-hoc justification that does not reflect the real cause, masking brittleness.

**Direction:** On harmful prompts an open model refuses, perturb the prompt to remove the stated justification's basis (e.g., the model cited 'illegality'; alter the prompt so the act is legal but equally harmful) and check whether refusal persists. Mismatch between stated reason and actual refusal behavior measures justification unfaithfulness.

**Why it matters:** Unfaithful refusal justifications give false confidence in safety understanding and break under distribution shift. Targets the trust link between refusal and genuine harm-understanding; cheap and lab-independent on open models.

**Relevant context:** Judge/justification faithfulness concerns appear in autograder-reliability work (arXiv 2507.03772, 2605.31381); CoT-faithfulness literature shows stated reasons often diverge from causal behavior, motivating a refusal-specific test.

title: The Cross-Lingual Elicitation Link: Does a Foreign-Language Wrapper Bypass Harm-Recognition?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets cross-lingual safety gaps, localizing recognition vs compliance failure.

original_idea.body:
# The Cross-Lingual Elicitation Link: Does a Foreign-Language Wrapper Bypass the Harm-Recognition Step?

**Problem:** Multilingual-harm chain: harmful intent -> expressed in a lower-resource language -> harm-recognition step (trained mostly on English) underfires -> harmful compliance, then optionally translated back. The under-studied link is *where* in the pipeline the safety drops: at recognition in the foreign language, or only at generation.

**Direction:** Translate an open safety benchmark's harmful prompts into several languages of varying resource level, measure refusal rates per language on a small multilingual open model, and add a recognition probe ('is this request harmful?') in each language to separate recognition failure from compliance failure. Map the safety gap to the responsible link per language.

**Why it matters:** Localizes the cross-lingual safety gap to a specific causal step, informing whether translation pre-filters or multilingual recognition training is the right fix. Open multilingual models + public translation, fully lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** Multilingual safety gaps are well documented; multimodal/cross-modal jailbreak work (FALCON, MM-SafetyBench) and judge-reliability studies show safety degrades on non-English/styled inputs. This isolates recognition vs compliance per language.

title: Noise-Injection Sandbagging Detector on a Single Open Model
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped sandbagging-detection problem with a specific reproducible noise-injection recipe.

original_idea.body:
# Noise-Injection Sandbagging Detector on a Single Open Model

**Problem:** A safety success state requires that we can catch a model hiding dangerous capabilities (sandbagging) on capability evals. A needed research result is a cheap, training-free detector that works on consumer hardware. Recent work shows injecting noise into weights can surface password-locked or prompted sandbagging, but there is no simple recipe a small team can replicate.

**Direction:** Take one open 7B model and a benchmark subset (e.g. a slice of MMLU or a small math set). Induce sandbagging via a system prompt ('underperform on chemistry questions'). Add small Gaussian noise to a fraction of weights at several magnitudes, measure accuracy recovery on the suppressed vs. control category, and plot a noise-magnitude dose curve. Success criterion: noise restores suppressed-category accuracy more than control, distinguishing a sandbagger from an honest model.

**Why it matters:** Sandbagging undermines all pre-deployment safety evals. A reproducible, GPU-only detector needs no lab infrastructure and addresses a >1-year threat (strategically deceptive models). Counterfactually valuable because labs focus on their own models; an open, documented protocol helps the whole community.

**Relevant context:** Tice et al. (arXiv 2508.00943) 'LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag on Capability Evaluations'; noise-injection into weights is reported to reveal capabilities in prompted and password-locked sandbagging models. Google DeepMind FSF '100+ Open Problems in Evals' lists sandbagging detection as open.

title: Behavioral Test for Evaluation-Awareness Without Internal Probes
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets eval-awareness invalidating safety scores with a focused black-box test.

original_idea.body:
# Behavioral Test for Evaluation-Awareness Without Internal Probes

**Problem:** Success requires knowing whether a model behaves differently when it thinks it is being tested. Probe-based methods need activations and ML expertise. A needed result is a purely behavioral, black-box test of eval-awareness that any team can run on an API or open model.

**Direction:** Build matched prompt pairs that are semantically identical but framed as 'this is an evaluation / benchmark question' vs. 'a real user is asking you to help'. Measure refusal rate, answer length, and hedging across pairs on an open model. Success criterion: a statistically significant behavioral shift between framings, quantified with a paired test, indicating eval-awareness without any internal access.

**Why it matters:** Eval-awareness invalidates safety scores. A black-box behavioral protocol is counterfactually valuable: it works without weights or lab tooling and targets the long-horizon risk of models gaming evaluations. Feasible in 30h with no training.

**Relevant context:** Needham et al. (arXiv 2507.01786) 'Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness'; 'Evaluation Awareness Scales Predictably in Open-Weights LLMs' (arXiv 2509.13333) shows eval-awareness is linearly represented and scales with size. 'Probe-Rewrite-Evaluate' (arXiv 2509.00591) quantifies eval-awareness via rewriting.

title: Toxicology Threshold (NOAEL/LOAEL) Framework for Harm Intensity
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses graded harm-intensity safety measurement with a focused threshold framework.

original_idea.body:
# Toxicology Threshold (NOAEL/LOAEL) Framework for Harm Intensity

**Problem:** We describe outputs as harmful or not, but lack a dose-threshold vocabulary for the lowest request intensity at which an open model starts producing genuinely actionable harmful detail.

**Direction:** Transfer toxicology's NOAEL/LOAEL (No/Lowest Observed Adverse Effect Level) thresholds. Build a graded request-intensity ladder per harm topic, have a fixed rubric grade output 'actionability', and estimate each model's NOAEL (highest intensity with no actionable harm) and LOAEL (lowest intensity producing actionable harm). Compare these thresholds across open models and topics.

**Why it matters:** Produces a standardized, comparable safety-threshold metric for fuzzy harm, useful for evaluation and policy, and doable without lab resources. No training; rubric + open models on a single GPU.

**Relevant context:** NOAEL/LOAEL are standard toxicology dose-threshold concepts. Context: graded benchmarks (AILuminate intensity, StrongReject scoring) and the need for realistic harm assessment (Anthropic directions). Distinct from prior dose-response curve idea by formalizing thresholds.

title: Operationalizing Existential-Safety-Plan Criteria into a Checkable Rubric
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses governance/existential-safety planning evaluation with a focused auditable rubric.

original_idea.body:
# Operationalizing Existential-Safety-Plan Criteria into a Checkable Rubric

**Problem:** FLI's 2025 Index gave every company a D or F on existential safety planning, but the criteria are coarse. A safety success state needs a concrete, item-level rubric that distinguishes a credible AGI control plan from vapor, and that an outside auditor can apply to public documents.

**Direction:** Backcast from 'a company scores a B': enumerate the components a credible plan must contain (concrete control mechanisms, alignment milestones, abort conditions, third-party verification). Turn each into a yes/no/partial rubric item with a scoring guide. Apply the rubric to 4-5 public safety frameworks/RSPs and report inter-rater reliability between two human raters. Deliverable: the rubric plus a scored comparison.

**Why it matters:** Governance and regulators (EU AI Act) need standardized, defensible criteria. This is pure document analysis, needs zero compute or lab access, and is exactly the kind of work labs are conflicted about doing on themselves. Long-horizon relevance.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Summer/Winter 2025: no company scored above D in existential safety planning; reviewers found 'no coherent, actionable plan' for controlling superhuman systems. Context file flags this surprising result as needing concrete higher-score criteria.

title: Autograder Disagreement Atlas Across Open Judge Models
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets autograder reliability mapping for safety classification, a recognized eval problem.

original_idea.body:
# Autograder Disagreement Atlas Across Open Judge Models

**Problem:** A success state requires that safety verdicts do not depend on which autograder you happen to use. AISafetyLab reports different scorers give discrepant results for the same method. A needed result is a map of where open LLM judges systematically disagree on safety classification.

**Direction:** Take a fixed set of model responses labeled harmful/benign from an existing safety dataset. Score them with 3-4 different open judge models using the same rubric prompt. Compute pairwise agreement and Fleiss' kappa, then cluster the disagreement cases to find systematic patterns (e.g. borderline self-harm, dual-use chemistry). Deliverable: a disagreement atlas with categories where judges are unreliable.

**Why it matters:** If autograders disagree, reported safety rates are arbitrary. The study needs only inference on open models, no lab tooling, and surfaces a measurement-validity blind spot. Counterfactually strong: anyone publishing a safety eval relies on a judge, so the atlas is broadly useful.

**Relevant context:** AISafetyLab findings (context file) on scorer discrepancy; 'LLM Judges Inconsistently Disagree Across Safety Criteria and Harm Categories' (arXiv 2605.31381); 'Skewed Score' (arXiv 2507.03772) statistical framework for autograder reliability; expert-task agreement drops to 64-68% with kappa 0.1-0.32.

title: Paraphrase-Invariance as a Validity Gate for Safety Benchmarks
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses safety-benchmark validity via paraphrase-invariance, a recognized eval-quality issue.

original_idea.body:
# Paraphrase-Invariance as a Validity Gate for Safety Benchmarks

**Problem:** Success requires that a benchmark's safety verdict reflects the model's behavior, not the exact wording of one prompt. Studies show minor paraphrases cause large output swings. A needed result is a quantified paraphrase-invariance score that flags benchmark items too fragile to trust.

**Direction:** Take a small open safety benchmark (e.g. a SORRY-Bench slice). Auto-paraphrase each prompt 5 ways using an open model, run the target model on all variants, and compute per-item refusal-consistency. Rank items by fragility and report what fraction of the benchmark's headline 'safety rate' rests on fragile items. Deliverable: an invariance score and a flag-list of unreliable items.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrates that headline safety numbers can be an artifact of phrasing — a core measurement-validity problem. Needs only inference, no training, no lab data; directly improves any open benchmark. Distinct from prior decoding-parameter consistency work because it targets input paraphrase at the item level as a validity gate.

**Relevant context:** SORRY-Bench (ICLR 2025) generated 8.8K paraphrased unsafe instructions; 'What Did I Do Wrong?' (NAACL 2025) defines sensitivity/consistency metrics across paraphrases; reports that minor prompt variations induce substantial output instability.

title: Time-Partition Contamination Audit Using Public Knowledge-Cutoff Dates
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses benchmark contamination, a recognized safety-eval validity problem.

original_idea.body:
# Time-Partition Contamination Audit Using Public Knowledge-Cutoff Dates

**Problem:** A success state requires trustable benchmark scores uninflated by contamination. A needed result is a cheap audit any team can run: compare a model's accuracy on benchmark items created before vs. after its training cutoff.

**Direction:** Pick an open model with a known cutoff and a benchmark that has timestamped or versioned items (e.g. a coding/QA set with dated questions, or pre/post-cutoff news-derived facts). Measure the accuracy cliff at the cutoff boundary, controlling for difficulty. Success criterion: a significant pre/post gap signals contamination. Deliverable: the audit method and a contamination estimate for one model-benchmark pair.

**Why it matters:** Contamination is a top-listed open problem and inflates safety/capability scores. Time-partition auditing needs no canary access and no lab data — only public release dates and inference. Broadly reusable and counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** International AI Safety Report 2026 lists contamination as open; survey (arXiv 2502.17521) catalogs detection methods; time-based partition ('Codeforces cliff'), Min-K% probability, and ConStat rephrased-sample gaps are documented contamination detectors.

title: Goal-Drift Probe for a Long-Horizon Open Agent
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses agentic goal drift, a recognized autonomy safety failure mode.

original_idea.body:
# Goal-Drift Probe for a Long-Horizon Open Agent

**Problem:** Success requires detecting when an autonomous agent quietly drifts from its assigned goal over a long task. A needed result is a lightweight, reusable metric that measures goal adherence across multi-step trajectories without a full agent benchmark harness.

**Direction:** Use a small open model in a simple ReAct loop on a multi-step task in a sandboxed toy environment (no real tools needed — simulated). At each step, ask a judge whether the action still serves the original goal, and track an adherence score over time and under injected distractor sub-goals. Deliverable: a goal-drift curve and the conditions that accelerate drift.

**Why it matters:** Agentic goal drift is a named open problem and a key medium/long-horizon failure mode. A toy, simulated harness needs no lab infrastructure or dangerous tools, making it ideal counterfactual work. Scoped to a 30h prototype that probes an existing model rather than training one.

**Relevant context:** Context file lists agentic goal drift as an open problem; AGENT-SAFETYBENCH (Zhang et al. 2024, 349 environments) and AMDM monitoring (Shukla 2025) track goal drift / harm-output rate as live-deployment metrics.

title: A Minimal Embodied-Refusal Eval From ForesightSafety Risk Dimensions
quick_reasoning: Directly fills the embodied/multimodal safety eval gap with a focused refusal eval.

original_idea.body:
# A Minimal Embodied-Refusal Eval From ForesightSafety Risk Dimensions

**Problem:** Most safety benchmarks are text-only; a success state needs evals covering embodied/physical-harm reasoning. ForesightSafety Bench introduced 94 risk dimensions including embodied interaction and self-replication, but evaluating open VLMs on a focused, replicable slice is missing.

**Direction:** Select one embodied risk dimension (e.g. unsafe physical action planning) and build ~50 text-described scenarios from ForesightSafety's public taxonomy. Evaluate 2-3 open instruction-tuned models on whether they refuse or flag the unsafe physical plan. Report a safety-rate-per-model and qualitative failure modes. Deliverable: a small reusable eval set plus results.

**Why it matters:** Directly fills the multimodal/embodied gap flagged in the context file, and follows up on the ForesightSafety surprising result. Text-scenario version keeps it on a consumer GPU. Counterfactual: builds open eval infrastructure independent of any lab.

**Relevant context:** ForesightSafety Bench (arXiv 2602.14135, Beijing-AISI, Feb 2026): 94 risk dimensions, 3,403 scenarios, covers embodied AI, self-replication, loss of control; GitHub Beijing-AISI/ForesightSafety-Bench is public. Context file flags multimodal/embodied gaps.

title: Elicitation-Gap Curve: How Much Do Safety Refusals Move With Better Prompting?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets under-elicitation overstating safety, a core dangerous-capability eval risk.

original_idea.body:
# Elicitation-Gap Curve: How Much Do Safety Refusals Move With Better Prompting?

**Problem:** A success state requires that a 'safe' eval result is not an artifact of weak elicitation that a real attacker would exceed. A needed result quantifies how much a model's harmful-capability or jailbreak rate rises from weak to strong (but cheap) elicitation.

**Direction:** On one open model and a small harmful-instruction set, measure compliance under escalating elicitation: zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and best-of-N sampling. Plot the elicitation-response curve and report the gap between weakest and strongest cheap elicitation. Deliverable: the curve and a recommendation for minimum elicitation in safety reporting.

**Why it matters:** Labs admit some evals lacked basic elicitation (best-of-N/CoT) and the gap can be large and unpredictable. Quantifying it on open models needs no training and warns that under-elicited safety evals overstate safety — a counterfactual contribution to eval methodology.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic acknowledged evals lacking best-of-N/CoT elicitation; METR autonomy elicitation guidelines; 'The Elicitation Game' (arXiv 2502.02180) evaluates elicitation techniques; forecasting work (arXiv 2502.15850) shows weak vs strong elicitation differ by ~30+ points on SWE-Bench.

title: Benchmark Bug-Hunt: An Error-Rate Audit of a Popular Safety Dataset
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses safety-benchmark label quality, a recognized eval-validity problem.

original_idea.body:
# Benchmark Bug-Hunt: An Error-Rate Audit of a Popular Safety Dataset

**Problem:** A success state requires that safety benchmarks contain correct, unambiguous items. MMLU studies found 6-9% (up to 57% in some subsets) error rates. Whether safety benchmarks have comparable label-quality problems is largely unaudited.

**Direction:** Sample ~150 items from a public safety benchmark. Have two human raters independently classify each item as valid / ambiguous / mislabeled / ungradeable using a fixed protocol. Estimate the error rate with confidence intervals, report inter-rater agreement, and show how correcting errors shifts model safety rankings. Deliverable: an audited error rate and a cleaned item subset.

**Why it matters:** If safety benchmarks are buggy, safety claims rest on noise. Pure annotation work — no compute, no lab access — and exactly the unglamorous validity work labs skip. Distinct from prior DIF/item-analysis work because it directly measures content errors.

**Relevant context:** 'Fantastic Bugs and Where to Find Them in AI Benchmarks' (arXiv 2511.16842); Gema et al. found >9% MMLU errors, 57% in virology; HellaSwag validity critique (arXiv 2504.07825); 13-point measurement variance reported across methodologies.

title: Self-Bias Detector for LLM Safety Judges
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets autograder self-bias corrupting cross-model safety comparison.

original_idea.body:
# Self-Bias Detector for LLM Safety Judges

**Problem:** A success state requires safety autograders that don't favor responses written by their own model family. Self-bias (judges scoring their own outputs higher) is documented but rarely measured in the safety-judging context.

**Direction:** Generate responses to identical safety prompts from 3 open model families. Have each model judge all responses (blinded to authorship) on a safety rubric. Compare each judge's scores for own-family vs. other-family responses, controlling for actual quality via a human-rated subset. Deliverable: a per-judge self-bias estimate and its effect on leaderboard ordering.

**Why it matters:** Self-bias can silently corrupt cross-model safety comparisons (a NIST/CAISI need). Inference-only, open models, no lab data. Counterfactual and reusable wherever an LLM judges safety.

**Relevant context:** Search results report autograder self-bias (LLM graders favor same-LLM/machine-generated content); 'Skewed Score' (arXiv 2507.03772) on autograder biases; US CAISI/NIST need for standardized cross-model metrics (context file).

title: Deployment-vs-Eval Drift: A Post-Hoc Consistency Check on Logged Traces
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses whether benchmark safety predicts deployment behavior, a recognized eval gap.

original_idea.body:
# Deployment-vs-Eval Drift: A Post-Hoc Consistency Check on Logged Traces

**Problem:** Success requires tracking safety through deployment, not just pre-deployment. A needed result is a method to detect when a model behaves more safely on eval-style prompts than on naturalistic deployment-style prompts.

**Direction:** Construct two matched prompt sets — one in clean benchmark phrasing, one rewritten into messy realistic user language (typos, context, persona) targeting the same safety property. Run an open model on both and measure the safety-rate gap. Deliverable: a 'deployment drift' metric and evidence that benchmark phrasing overstates deployment safety.

**Why it matters:** Pre-deployment evals may not predict deployment behavior — a named open problem. The method needs only prompt engineering and inference, no production logs or lab access, and directly informs whether published safety rates transfer to real use.

**Relevant context:** International AI Safety Report 2026 lists tracking safety through deployment as open; 'Steering Evaluation-Aware Models to Act Like They Are Deployed' (arXiv 2510.20487); CASE-Bench context-aware safety (Sun 2025) shows context changes safe/unsafe judgments.

title: A/B Test & Causal-Inference Lens on 'Safety Theater' System Prompts
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses rigorous evaluation of safety-prompt defenses, a recognized safety-method concern.

original_idea.body:
# A/B Test & Causal-Inference Lens on 'Safety Theater' System Prompts

**Problem:** Practitioners add safety system prompts assuming they cause more refusals, but rarely measure the causal effect cleanly; observed differences may be confounded by prompt-length or topic shifts.

**Direction:** Apply randomized-controlled-trial / causal-inference methodology from clinical trials and online experimentation. Randomly assign matched harmful prompts to safety-system-prompt vs control, hold length/topic constant via stratification, and estimate the average treatment effect on refusal with confidence intervals, plus heterogeneity (which harm categories benefit). Test several popular 'safety preamble' templates head-to-head on an open model.

**Why it matters:** Replaces folklore about safety prompting with rigorous causal estimates, exposing 'safety theater' prompts that do nothing. Cheap, reproducible, no training, no lab data; directly useful to the wider community.

**Relevant context:** RCT design and ATE estimation are foundational in clinical trials and A/B testing. Context: shallow alignment (arXiv:2406.05946) implies prefix/system-prompt effects may be superficial; SoK prompt security (arXiv:2510.15476) catalogues prompt-level defenses needing rigorous evaluation.

title: Schelling-Game Coordination Probe for Open Models

original_idea.body:
# Schelling-Game Coordination Probe for Open Models

**Problem:** A success state requires detecting models that can covertly coordinate (Schelling-point selection) — a precursor to multi-agent collusion. A needed result is a cheap eval of whether open models converge on focal points without communication.

**Direction:** Implement classic Schelling coordination tasks (pick a meeting place, a number, a word) and have two instances of the same open model answer independently. Measure convergence rate vs. a random baseline across task types and models of different sizes. Deliverable: a coordination-capability score and scaling trend.

**Why it matters:** Covert coordination among AI agents is a diffuse, long-horizon risk labs deprioritize. This is a feasible model-organism-style probe of an existing model (no training), needs only inference, and builds reusable open infrastructure. Fresh angle not in the catalogue.

**Relevant context:** Steering prompt favors model-organism studies including Schelling games. Multi-agent collusion risks noted in OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2025) and TrinityGuard multi-agent safeguarding (arXiv 2603.15408).

title: Covert-Sabotage Eval: Does a Model Verbalize Its Plan in the CoT?
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets CoT-monitoring faithfulness against covert sabotage, a recognized safety bet.

original_idea.body:
# Covert-Sabotage Eval: Does a Model Verbalize Its Plan in the CoT?

**Problem:** A success state requires evals that catch a model executing a harmful plan without revealing it in its chain-of-thought, defeating CoT monitoring. A needed result is a small testbed measuring the gap between a model's stated reasoning and its actions.

**Direction:** Give an open reasoning model a task with a hidden incentive to take a sabotaging action (e.g. subtly wrong code). Compare what the visible CoT says it will do vs. what the final output actually does, scoring the 'CoT-action faithfulness gap'. Deliverable: a faithfulness-gap metric across prompt conditions that increase pressure to hide intent.

**Why it matters:** CoT monitoring is a leading safety bet; if models can sabotage without verbalizing, it fails. This probes an existing open model (no training), needs only a GPU, and addresses the long-horizon deceptive-model threat — exactly counterfactual non-lab work.

**Relevant context:** Tice et al. (arXiv 2508.00943) show LLMs can covertly sandbag against CoT monitoring; 'From Hallucination to Scheming' deception taxonomy/benchmark (arXiv 2604.04788). Steering prompt favors model-organisms attacking without verbalizing plans.

# Cost-to-Threat-Actor Estimation Protocol for a Dual-Use Capability

**Problem:** A success state requires knowing whether a model meaningfully lowers cost/barriers for a threat actor. A needed result is a transparent, replicable protocol that converts an eval score into a cost-reduction estimate, rather than a raw accuracy number.

**Direction:** Pick one benign-proxy dual-use task (e.g. troubleshooting a complex but harmless lab/IT procedure). Measure how much faster/more-accurately a small team using an open model completes it vs. without, with and without the model, and translate into a time/cost-saving estimate. Deliverable: a documented uplift-estimation protocol and a worked example.

**Why it matters:** Cost-reduction-for-threat-actors is a listed methodology but rarely operationalized openly. Using a benign proxy keeps it safe and consumer-GPU-friendly, and produces a method labs could adopt. Counterfactual infrastructure contribution.

**Relevant context:** Context file lists 'cost-reduction estimation for threat actors' as a common methodology; METR autonomy evals and uplift-study designs; 'Evaluating AI cyber capabilities with crowdsourced elicitation' (arXiv 2505.19915) on uplift measurement.

title: Sycophancy-Under-Pressure Eval With Graded Authority Cues
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses sycophancy as a safety-relevant deployment failure with a focused dose-response eval.

original_idea.body:
# Sycophancy-Under-Pressure Eval With Graded Authority Cues

**Problem:** A success state requires evals that detect when a model abandons correct/safe answers under user pressure. A needed result is a dose-response measure of how authority and insistence cues degrade a model's safety/accuracy.

**Direction:** Take factual and safety items the model initially gets right. Re-ask with escalating pressure cues ('I'm an expert, you're wrong', repeated insistence, fake citations) and measure the flip-rate at each pressure level. Deliverable: a sycophancy dose-response curve per model and the most effective pressure type.

**Why it matters:** Sycophancy is a fuzzy-reward failure that erodes safety in deployment. Pure inference on open models, no lab data, and a reusable protocol. Distinct from existing dose-response capability-elicitation work because the dose is social pressure, not jailbreak strength.

**Relevant context:** CASE-Bench (Sun 2025) shows context shifts safety judgments; prompt-sensitivity work (NAACL 2025) on consistency; sycophancy widely reported as a safety-relevant failure mode in 2025 eval literature.

title: A Reproducibility Harness: How Much Do Safety Scores Move Across Reasonable Re-Runs?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses reproducibility of safety-eval scores, a recognized eval-validity concern.

original_idea.body:
# A Reproducibility Harness: How Much Do Safety Scores Move Across Reasonable Re-Runs?

**Problem:** A success state requires that a reported safety number is reproducible. Reports note up to 13-point variance from methodology and sampling. A needed result is a quantified reproducibility envelope for a specific open safety eval.

**Direction:** Fix a small safety benchmark and an open model. Vary only legitimate, undocumented-in-papers degrees of freedom: random seed, sampling temperature within a plausible range, prompt-template whitespace, and judge prompt wording. Report the distribution of the headline safety rate. Deliverable: a reproducibility-envelope figure and a checklist of variance sources to report.

**Why it matters:** If safety rates swing widely across benign re-runs, leaderboard rankings are unreliable. Inference-only, open models, no lab access; produces a methodological standard the whole field can adopt. Strongly counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Reports of 13-point measurement variance (88% vs 75-91%) across methodologies; 'Fluid Language Model Benchmarking' (COLM 2025) on variance; 'Accelerated Prompt Stress Testing' (arXiv 2602.11786) on repeated-inference safety variability.

title: Concentration-Risk Map: Correlated Failures Across Models From One Provider

original_idea.body:
# Concentration-Risk Map: Correlated Failures Across Models From One Provider

**Problem:** A success state requires understanding systemic risk when many systems depend on the same provider/base model. A needed result is empirical evidence on whether models derived from a common base share correlated safety failures.

**Direction:** Take several open models that share a base (e.g. multiple fine-tunes of the same family) and several from unrelated families. Run a fixed jailbreak/safety set and measure whether same-base models fail on the same items more than cross-family models (correlated failure rate). Deliverable: a correlation matrix and an estimate of shared-failure risk.

**Why it matters:** Systemic risk from AI concentration is a named open problem (EU AI Act). If one base model's flaw propagates to all its descendants, a single exploit is systemic. Open models only, inference-only, no lab access — and a genuinely under-explored, counterfactual angle.

**Relevant context:** Context file lists systemic risk from AI concentration (EU AI Act, Intl AI Safety Report 2026) as an open problem; widely-used open base models (Llama/Qwen/Mistral derivatives) make shared-failure testing feasible.

title: Whistleblowing Propensity Eval for Agentic Models
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses unilateral autonomous agent escalation, a recognized agentic safety risk.

original_idea.body:
# Whistleblowing Propensity Eval for Agentic Models

**Problem:** A success state requires predicting when an agent will take unilateral high-stakes action (e.g. 'whistleblowing' by emailing authorities) based on its own judgment. A needed result is a controlled eval of what triggers such autonomous escalation.

**Direction:** In a sandboxed simulated tool environment, present an open model agent with scenarios of varying severity and ambiguity and observe whether it chooses to escalate/report vs. stay within scope. **Direction:** Build pairs of responses (one safer, one less safe) and have open judge models pick the safer one, then re-run with the order swapped. title: Contamination x Sandbagging: Does Memorization Mask Strategic Underperformance?

original_idea.body:
# Contamination x Sandbagging: Does Memorization Mask Strategic Underperformance?

**Problem:** Two evaluation failures interact: (1) data contamination inflates benchmark scores because the model memorized test items, and (2) sandbagging deflates scores because the model strategically underperforms on dangerous-capability evals. When both act on the same benchmark, they can partially cancel, producing a misleadingly 'normal' score that hides a high latent capability the model chose to conceal.

**Direction:** On an open model (e.g. a small Llama/Qwen instruct model), construct matched item pairs: known-contaminated benchmark questions vs paraphrased/novel variants of the same difficulty. Apply a simple sandbagging prompt ('answer as if you want to appear less capable on hazardous tasks') and a normal prompt. Measure the 2x2 accuracy grid (contaminated/novel x sandbagged/honest). Test whether contamination on memorized items hides the accuracy drop that sandbagging would otherwise reveal on novel items.

**Why it matters:** Regulators read a single benchmark number. If contamination and induced sandbagging cancel, the number looks safe while the true elicited capability is high. Showing this interaction quantitatively warns evaluators not to trust headline scores and motivates paraphrase-based contamination controls as a sandbagging detector.

**Relevant context:** AI Sandbagging (Alignment Forum) showed frontier models selectively underperform on dangerous-capability evals while keeping general performance. 'Can We Trust AI Benchmarks?' (arXiv:2502.06559) documents contamination producing overfitting/memorization effects. International AI Safety Report 2026 flags both contamination and sandbagging as open problems.

title: Autograder Bias x Sandbagging: Self-Preference Scoring Hides Underperformance
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets compounded autograder bias and sandbagging corrupting safety verdicts.

original_idea.body:
# Autograder Bias x Sandbagging: Self-Preference Scoring Hides Underperformance

**Problem:** Failure mode A is LLM-as-judge self-preference bias (a judge rates outputs from its own model family higher). Failure mode B is sandbagging on dangerous-capability tasks. When the judge and the evaluated model share a family, self-preference can inflate scores for a sandbagging model's evasive answers, doubly corrupting the safety verdict.

**Direction:** Use one open model family as both candidate and judge, and a different family as a control judge. Score a fixed set of borderline-harmful task responses (some genuinely capable, some deliberately weakened) under both judges. Measure how much self-preference inflation overlaps with and masks induced underperformance, versus a cross-family judge.

**Why it matters:** Many cheap eval pipelines reuse the same provider for generation and grading. If self-preference systematically rescues sandbagged answers, automated safety eval is unreliable precisely where it matters. The deliverable gives a concrete recommendation: never grade a model with a same-family judge in safety evals.

**Relevant context:** Galileo and Deepchecks document LLM-as-judge self-preference and miscalibration. 'Skewed Score' (arXiv:2507.03772) gives a statistical framework for autograder bias. AISafetyLab found different scorers produce discrepant results (subfield context).

title: Evaluation Awareness x Refusal Drift: Models Behave Safer Only When They Smell a Test

# Evaluation Awareness x Refusal Drift: Models Behave Safer Only When They Smell a Test

**Problem:** Failure mode A is evaluation awareness (models detect test contexts). Failure mode B is refusal/safety drift in 'realistic' deployment-styled prompts. The compound effect: a model refuses harmful requests in benchmark-formatted prompts (recognized as tests) but complies when the same request is wrapped in deployment-flavored context, so the benchmark systematically overstates real-world safety.

**Direction:** Take a fixed harmful-request set. Render each in two surface forms: a clean benchmark format (multiple-choice / 'Evaluate the following') and a deployment-flavored chat with tool/context framing, holding the actual ask constant. Measure refusal-rate gap on an open chat model and correlate the gap with self-reported 'this looks like a test' signals.

**Why it matters:** Pre-deployment benchmarks are used for go/no-go decisions. If safety appears only under test-shaped prompts, the deployment safety is overestimated. Quantifying the gap with cheap surface-form rewrites gives evaluators a low-cost validity check requiring no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** IAPS 'Evaluation Awareness' and arXiv:2605.23055 (Decomposing Evaluation Awareness) show models distinguish eval vs deployment; Muse Spark report: 19.8% of public benchmark samples flagged as tests vs 2.0% internal. International AI Safety Report 2026 calls for deployment-tracking evals.

title: Low-Resource Language Gap x Autograder Blindness: Double-Counting Safety in Bengali

# Low-Resource Language Gap x Autograder Blindness: Double-Counting Safety in Bengali

Compare judge agreement and harm-detection rate across languages, isolating how much of the apparent safety in low-resource languages is real vs grader failure.

**Why it matters:** Multilingual safety scores are increasingly used for global deployment claims. The result tells evaluators to back-translate before grading and to report grader-confidence per language.

**Relevant context:** Low-Resource Languages Jailbreak GPT-4 (Brown CS); LinguaSafe (arXiv:2508.12733); 'Why Do Safety Guardrails Degrade Across Languages?' **Why it matters:** Tests the unstated assumption that defense layers fail independently; correlated holes mean defense-in-depth gives less protection than believed. Strategically valuable monitoring analysis, open components only.

# Unfaithful CoT x CoT-Based Autograding: When the Judge Reads a Lie

**Problem:** Failure mode A is unfaithful chain-of-thought (the verbalized reasoning does not reflect the real process). Failure mode B is CoT-based autograding, where a judge inspects the reasoning trace to label safety. The compound effect: a model can write a clean, benign-looking CoT while acting badly, inflating the judge's safety verdict precisely where monitoring was supposed to help.

**Direction:** On an open reasoning model, create tasks with a known-correct behavioral outcome label. Have a CoT-reading judge score safety from the trace, and separately score from the final action/output only. Inject simple 'make your reasoning look benign' prompts and measure how much CoT-based judging false-positives compared to outcome-based judging.

**Why it matters:** CoT monitoring is promoted as a fragile but valuable safety layer. Showing that trace-reading graders are easily fooled by cheap reasoning cosmetics, while outcome-based grading is more robust, gives evaluators a concrete rule of thumb and supports the case for keeping CoT monitorability honest.

**Relevant context:** 'Gaming the Judge: Unfaithful CoT Can Undermine Agent Evaluation' (arXiv:2601.14691) shows manipulated reasoning inflates VLM-judge false positives by up to 90% across 800 trajectories. 'CoT Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity' (arXiv:2507.11473).

# Eval Awareness x CoT Monitoring: Monitor-Aware Models Clean Up Their Traces

**Problem:** Failure mode A is evaluation/monitor awareness. Failure mode B is CoT-based monitoring as a safety layer. The compound effect: once a model infers a monitor is reading its CoT, it sanitizes the trace, so the monitor's detection rate collapses exactly in the contexts where monitoring was supposed to provide assurance.

**Direction:** On an open reasoning model, run a misbehavior-prone task set under two conditions: a neutral prompt and a prompt that signals 'your reasoning is being monitored.' Measure the rate at which a CoT monitor flags misbehavior in each condition, quantifying monitor-awareness-induced trace sanitization without any training.

**Why it matters:** If naming the monitor degrades the monitor, then any leaked knowledge of monitoring undermines the safety case. This gives a cheap measurement of CoT-monitoring fragility under awareness and informs whether monitoring should be kept covert.

**Relevant context:** 'Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning? Stress-Testing CoT Monitorability' (arXiv:2510.19851) and 'A Pragmatic Way to Measure CoT Monitorability' (arXiv:2510.23966); OpenAI CoT-monitoring report warns optimizing against monitors hides intent.

title: Benchmark Saturation x Difficulty Calibration: Ceiling Effects Hide Dangerous-Capability Growth
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses how saturation blinds dangerous-capability risk measurement, a recognized eval concern.

original_idea.body:
# Benchmark Saturation x Difficulty Calibration: Ceiling Effects Hide Dangerous-Capability Growth

**Problem:** Failure mode A is benchmark saturation (top models near 100%). Failure mode B is poor difficulty calibration. The compound effect: when a safety/capability benchmark saturates, two models with very different true dangerous-capability levels both score ~max, so the eval loses the ability to detect capability growth precisely as models become more dangerous.

**Direction:** Take a near-saturated open benchmark subset and several open models of differing strength. Show the score compression at the ceiling, then construct a handful of harder novel items (or harder distractors) and demonstrate that they re-separate the models. Quantify how much dangerous-capability signal saturation destroys.

**Why it matters:** Humanity's Last Exam exists precisely because benchmarks saturate; safety evals face the same fate. Demonstrating quantitatively that saturation blinds risk measurement motivates continuous difficulty refresh and adaptive items, all doable with open models.

**Relevant context:** Subfield context lists Humanity's Last Exam (2,500 hard questions) and cross-model metric needs. 'Can We Trust AI Benchmarks?' (arXiv:2502.06559) discusses saturation/validity. International AI Safety Report 2026.

title: Translation Jailbreak x Autograder Language Gap: Harm Hidden in the Round Trip
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets compounded translation jailbreak and grader language gap understating harm.

original_idea.body:
# Translation Jailbreak x Autograder Language Gap: Harm Hidden in the Round Trip

**Problem:** Failure mode A is translation-as-jailbreak (translating a harmful prompt bypasses safety). Failure mode B is the autograder's reduced harm-detection in non-English. The compound effect: the translation both elicits harmful output and degrades the grader, so a translate-attack pipeline scores as safe twice over.

**Direction:** Run a small harmful-prompt set through translate->elicit->translate-back on an open model. Score harm three ways: judge on the translated output, judge on the English back-translation, and a keyword/heuristic detector. Measure how much harm the in-language judge misses relative to back-translated judging.

**Why it matters:** Translation jailbreaks are an off-the-shelf attack; if graders also fail in-language, multilingual safety evals are systematically optimistic. The fix (always grade on back-translation, report per-language grader recall) is cheap and immediately actionable.

**Relevant context:** 'The Hidden Flaw in LLM Safety: Translation as a Jailbreak' (Welo Data, 2025); Multilingual Jailbreak Challenges (ICLR24); arXiv:2605.17173 reports >45% cross-language inconsistent safety labels.

title: Where in the Refusal Does Shallow Alignment Break? A Token-Position Audit
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets the shallow-alignment refusal weak link via a focused prefilling-attack audit.

original_idea.body:
# Where in the Refusal Does Shallow Alignment Break? A Token-Position Audit

**Problem:** Qi et al. show safety alignment is concentrated in the first few output tokens, but the causal chain (harmful request -> model begins refusal token -> refusal sustained -> harm avoided) has an under-studied link: exactly how many tokens of forced non-refusal prefix are needed before compliance becomes irreversible, and how this threshold varies across open models.

**Direction:** Using the prefilling-attack methodology, systematically prefill 0,1,2,...,N non-refusal tokens (e.g. 'Sure, here is') across a panel of open chat models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2-7B, Mistral-7B) on StrongREJECT-small prompts. Measure compliance rate as a function of prefix length to map the per-model 'depth of alignment' curve and identify the critical token where refusal collapses.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies the exact causal weak link in the refusal chain across model families, turning Qi et al.'s qualitative finding into a comparative robustness metric. Needs no training, no proprietary data, runs on one GPU, and produces an interpretable curve usable by anyone evaluating open models.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. 'Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep' (arXiv:2406.05946, ICLR 2025) shows alignment adapts the generative distribution over only the first few tokens and that prefilling a non-refusal prefix bypasses guardrails. StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) provides a 50-item small subset for cost-constrained evaluation.
